resources.string: A box and a line share three cells. If all positions for one digit in either house lie in that intersection, the digit is locked there. Pointing starts with the box; claiming starts with the row or column.
The starting house must contain this digit once. Its intersection therefore supplies the digit to the other house too, excluding every other position in that second house.
Check every remaining position for the digit in the starting house. Two or three aligned candidates are useful only when no other position remains there.

For one digit, find 2 rows whose remaining positions are confined to the same 2 columns. These rows are the base houses and the columns are the cover houses. A X-Wing also works with rows and columns exchanged.
The 2 base houses each need this digit. Their 2 copies must occupy different cover houses, filling all 2 of them. Remove the digit from each cover house outside the bases.
Count houses, not corners: a X-Wing does not need a candidate at every crossing. Check that none of the base houses has another position outside the 2 covers.

Start with a 2-by-2 X-Wing shape. Allow extra positions for the digit in its base houses: these are the fins. All fins must lie in one box. Possible eliminations must be in a cover house, outside the bases, and see every fin.
Consider both cases. If a fin is true, it excludes the target directly. If all fins are false, the remaining X-Wing excludes that same target. Only a candidate excluded in both cases can be removed.
Do not clear an entire cover line. Keep only targets that see every fin. A missing core position beside the fins is a sashimi case; the same two-case proof still has to work.

For one digit, find 3 rows whose remaining positions are confined to the same 3 columns. These rows are the base houses and the columns are the cover houses. A Swordfish also works with rows and columns exchanged.
The 3 base houses each need this digit. Their 3 copies must occupy different cover houses, filling all 3 of them. Remove the digit from each cover house outside the bases.
Count houses, not corners: a Swordfish does not need a candidate at every crossing. Check that none of the base houses has another position outside the 3 covers.

Start with a 3-by-3 Swordfish shape. Allow extra positions for the digit in its base houses: these are the fins. All fins must lie in one box. Possible eliminations must be in a cover house, outside the bases, and see every fin.

Consider both cases. If a fin is true, it excludes the target directly. If all fins are false, the remaining Swordfish excludes that same target. Only a candidate excluded in both cases can be removed.
Do not clear an entire cover line. Keep only targets that see every fin. A missing core position beside the fins is a sashimi case; the same two-case proof still has to work.

For one digit, find 4 rows whose remaining positions are confined to the same 4 columns. These rows are the base houses and the columns are the cover houses. A Jellyfish also works with rows and columns exchanged.
The 4 base houses each need this digit. Their 4 copies must occupy different cover houses, filling all 4 of them. Remove the digit from each cover house outside the bases.
Count houses, not corners: a Jellyfish does not need a candidate at every crossing. Check that none of the base houses has another position outside the 4 covers.

Start with a 4-by-4 Jellyfish shape. Allow extra positions for the digit in its base houses: these are the fins. All fins must lie in one box. Possible eliminations must be in a cover house, outside the bases, and see every fin.

Consider both cases. If a fin is true, it excludes the target directly. If all fins are false, the remaining Jellyfish excludes that same target. Only a candidate excluded in both cases can be removed.
Do not clear an entire cover line. Keep only targets that see every fin. A missing core position beside the fins is a sashimi case; the same two-case proof still has to work.
Find two parallel rows or columns that each contain exactly two positions for the same digit. Join one end from each pair along the perpendicular line. The two unjoined ends are the roofs.

Read the three links as strong–weak–strong. If one roof is false, its partner is true, the joined partner is false, and the other roof is true. At least one roof contains the digit, excluding it from their common peers.
Both walls must be conjugate pairs: exactly two positions in their respective lines. The joined floor only needs a weak link. If both roofs also line up, look for an X-Wing.
Use one conjugate pair in a row and another for the same digit in a column. One endpoint of each pair lies in the same box; connect those two endpoints with a weak link.
Starting from a false free end, follow strong–weak–strong to a true free end. At least one free end must be true, so remove the digit from cells that see both free ends.
Verify that the row and column each have exactly two positions. The middle box connection may be weak; the strings may cross visually without changing the proof.
A Crane joins a conjugate pair inside a box to a conjugate pair in a row or column, using a weak link between the pairs. All four candidates use the same digit.
The path is strong–weak–strong. Assuming either free endpoint false forces the other endpoint true. Any outside candidate that conflicts with both endpoints is therefore false.
Distinguish the strong box link from a pair that merely shares a box. The box must have exactly two remaining positions for that digit.
Inside one box, the positions for a digit lie on the arms of a row and a column, with their crossing empty of that digit. Connect this box pattern to a conjugate pair outside it.

Test the red candidate as true. It clears one arm of the box and one end of the external pair. The other end then becomes true and clears the other arm. The box has no place for the digit, so the assumption is false.
The empty rectangle concerns positions of one candidate, not empty cells. Check that every candidate in the box is on the two arms and that the external pair is genuinely strong.
Find three bivalue cells: a pivot {x,y} and wings {x,z} and {y,z}. Each wing sees the pivot. The common wing digit z is absent from the pivot.
If the pivot is x, the {x,z} wing must be z. If the pivot is y, the {y,z} wing must be z. Thus at least one wing is z; remove z from cells that see both wings.
All three pattern cells must have exactly two candidates. A target may have more candidates and need not see the pivot, but it must see both wings.
The pivot has exactly {x,y,z}; the wings have {x,z} and {y,z}. Both wings see the pivot. Unlike an XY-Wing, the common digit z can also occupy the pivot.
If the pivot is z, it supplies z itself. If it is x or y, one wing must supply z. At least one of all three pattern cells is z, so a target must see all three to lose z.
Do not use the wider XY-Wing elimination area. Seeing both wings is insufficient when the target cannot see the three-candidate pivot.

Use 4 cells and exactly 4 candidate digits, arranged as a pivot group and two wing groups. Cells within each group see one another; every wing cell sees every pivot cell. The two wings share only the elimination digit z.

If z is removed from every relevant pattern cell, 4 cells must use only 3 digits. The pivots exclude their digits from both wings; the wings cannot reuse any remaining digit between them. This leaves too few digits, so at least one relevant cell is z.

If z occurs in the pivot, a target must see every pattern occurrence of z. Otherwise it only needs to see all wing occurrences of z. Count the union of candidates, not the number of marks in one cell.

Use 5 cells and exactly 5 candidate digits, arranged as a pivot group and two wing groups. Cells within each group see one another; every wing cell sees every pivot cell. The two wings share only the elimination digit z.

If z is removed from every relevant pattern cell, 5 cells must use only 4 digits. The pivots exclude their digits from both wings; the wings cannot reuse any remaining digit between them. This leaves too few digits, so at least one relevant cell is z.

If z occurs in the pivot, a target must see every pattern occurrence of z. Otherwise it only needs to see all wing occurrences of z. Count the union of candidates, not the number of marks in one cell.

Use 6 cells and exactly 6 candidate digits, arranged as a pivot group and two wing groups. Cells within each group see one another; every wing cell sees every pivot cell. The two wings share only the elimination digit z.

If z is removed from every relevant pattern cell, 6 cells must use only 5 digits. The pivots exclude their digits from both wings; the wings cannot reuse any remaining digit between them. This leaves too few digits, so at least one relevant cell is z.

If z occurs in the pivot, a target must see every pattern occurrence of z. Otherwise it only needs to see all wing occurrences of z. Count the union of candidates, not the number of marks in one cell.

Use 7 cells and exactly 7 candidate digits, arranged as a pivot group and two wing groups. Cells within each group see one another; every wing cell sees every pivot cell. The two wings share only the elimination digit z.

If z is removed from every relevant pattern cell, 7 cells must use only 6 digits. The pivots exclude their digits from both wings; the wings cannot reuse any remaining digit between them. This leaves too few digits, so at least one relevant cell is z.

If z occurs in the pivot, a target must see every pattern occurrence of z. Otherwise it only needs to see all wing occurrences of z. Count the union of candidates, not the number of marks in one cell.

Find two non-peer bivalue cells with the same pair {x,y}. Find a house where every position for x is seen by at least one of these two cells. A conjugate pair is the simplest bridge, but a group can bridge them too.
The two bivalue cells cannot both be x: that would remove every x from the bridge house. At least one of them is y, so remove y from any cell that sees both.
Matching pairs alone are insufficient. Verify the bridge and its two visibility relationships. Either digit may serve as the bridge; the other digit is the elimination candidate.

For one digit, start from a conjugate pair and follow connected conjugate pairs. Alternate blue and orange at each link. Within this connected component, one entire colour is true and the other is false.

A candidate that sees both colours is false whichever colour wins (colour trap). If two candidates of one colour see each other, that whole colour is false and the opposite colour is true (colour contradiction).
Colour one connected component at a time. The same colour in an unrelated component has no shared meaning. The colours label hypotheses; they do not show the answer in advance.
Build a chain on one digit. Strong links carry false to true; weak links carry true to false. Alternate the two and start and end with strong links.

Assume the first endpoint false and follow the links: the last endpoint becomes true. At least one endpoint is true, excluding candidates that see both. In a closed chain, a repeated endpoint or a weak edge can also establish a placement or elimination.
A conjugate pair can supply either a strong or a weak link, as the path requires. Do not treat every same-digit pair in a house as strong. Check the actual endpoints of each recorded proof.

Extend an X-Chain by treating a group of same-digit candidates in a box–line intersection as one proposition: at least one member is true. A grouped strong link covers every remaining position in its house.

If all members of one group are false, a strongly linked group must contain a true member. A weak link between groups requires every member of one group to conflict with every member of the other. Alternate these implications to prove the two endpoint groups cannot both be false.
A true group does not mean all its cells contain the digit. A target must see every member of both endpoint groups. Overlapping groups must not be assumed to have a weak link.

Extend simple colouring to different digits. Use conjugate pairs in houses and the two candidates inside bivalue cells as either-or links. Alternate blue and orange across every such link in one connected component.

An uncoloured candidate that conflicts with both colours can be removed. A colour is impossible if it puts two values in one cell, repeats a digit in a house, or leaves a cell without any candidate. Its opposite colour then becomes true.
Conflicts mean either different digits in the same cell or the same digit in peer cells. Two unrelated candidates of different digits do not conflict merely because their cells see each other.
Join bivalue cells into a chain. Inside each cell, the two candidates form a strong link; between cells, matching digits provide weak links. Choose endpoints carrying the same digit.

If the first endpoint digit is false, the other candidate in its cell is true. Pass this constraint to the next bivalue cell and continue. The same digit at the far end becomes true, so it can be removed from common peers of the endpoints.
Every cell used for the internal strong links must have exactly two candidates. The endpoint digit must match. A closed XY-Chain can additionally eliminate candidates along its weak connections.
An Alternating Inference Chain can change digits inside a cell and continue along matching digits between cells. Alternate strong and weak implications, starting and ending with a strong link.

Starting with a false endpoint forces a true endpoint at the other end. Any candidate incompatible with both endpoints is false. When a chain returns to the same candidate, the resulting contradiction can instead prove that candidate true or false.

Strong means false implies true; weak means true implies false. They are logical properties, not just line styles. A target must conflict with both actual endpoint propositions, even when the endpoint digits differ.
Assume one candidate is true, then propagate only forced consequences. A true candidate excludes its competitors; a last remaining candidate in a cell or house becomes true.

If the assumption makes a candidate both true and false, empties a cell or a digit from a house, or creates a repeated value, it is impossible. Remove the original assumed candidate. The arrows show the recorded contradiction, not a guessed solution.
Keep every consequence conditional on the initial assumption. No contradiction means this particular chain proves nothing; it does not establish that the assumed candidate is correct.

Cover every alternative in one place: either every candidate in a cell, or every position for a digit in a house. Start one branch with each alternative true. At least one of these branches must describe the real solution.

Follow each branch using forced consequences. If every viable branch makes the same candidate true, place it; if every branch makes it false, remove it. A contradictory branch is impossible. The remaining branches must still cover all possibilities.
Do not omit an alternative that is inconvenient to follow. Separate branch colours label separate assumptions; facts derived under different assumptions cannot be combined into a single proof step.

A forcing net starts from all candidates of a cell or all positions of a digit in a house. Within one assumption, several consequence paths may split and later join. A join can require multiple earlier exclusions together.

For example, two paths may rule out x and y in one {x,y,z} cell, jointly forcing z. A single path alone is insufficient. Continue each complete net; only a consequence shared by every viable initial alternative is unconditional.

At each join, verify all incoming facts and keep them within the same assumption branch. Lines merely crossing on the board do not form a logical join. The proof text lists the combined premises explicitly.

Use only a classic Sudoku known to have one solution. Four unsolved corners in two rows, two columns and exactly two boxes cannot all be restricted to the same pair {a,b}: swapping a and b would create a second solution. Three corners contain only {a,b}; the fourth has extras.
If the fourth corner were a or b, all four corners would form the swappable pair. It must take an extra digit, so remove both a and b from that corner.
All four corners must be unsolved. A given cannot be swapped. Check exactly two boxes, not one or four.

Use only a classic Sudoku known to have one solution. Four unsolved corners in two rows, two columns and exactly two boxes cannot all be restricted to the same pair {a,b}: swapping a and b would create a second solution. Two aligned corners have only {a,b}; the other two each add the same single digit z.
The two extra corners cannot both choose from {a,b}. At least one is z, so z can be removed from every cell that sees both extra corners.
The two extra corners must add the same one digit. If they have different or several extras, this Type 2 argument no longer applies.

Use only a classic Sudoku known to have one solution. Four unsolved corners in two rows, two columns and exactly two boxes cannot all be restricted to the same pair {a,b}: swapping a and b would create a second solution. Two corners contain only {a,b}. The other two share a house and contain extra digits.

At least one extra digit must be used in the two extra corners. Treat their extras as one virtual cell; together with other cells in their shared house, it can complete a naked subset and eliminate that subset from the remaining cells.
Count the two-corner extras as one virtual cell when building the subset. Include every extra candidate and verify the other subset cells lie in the same house.

Use only a classic Sudoku known to have one solution. Four unsolved corners in two rows, two columns and exactly two boxes cannot all be restricted to the same pair {a,b}: swapping a and b would create a second solution. Two corners contain only {a,b}. The other two contain extras and form a conjugate pair on a in their shared house.
The strong link forces one extra corner to be a. If the other were b, the rectangle would be deadly. Remove b from both extra corners; retain the strongly linked digit a.
The conjugate pair must use one of the deadly-pair digits in the house shared by the extra corners. Merely seeing each other is not enough.

Use only a classic Sudoku known to have one solution. Four unsolved corners in two rows, two columns and exactly two boxes cannot all be restricted to the same pair {a,b}: swapping a and b would create a second solution. The only extra digit is z. It appears in two diagonal corners or in three corners; the other corners contain only {a,b}.
To avoid the swappable pair, at least one corner containing z must actually be z. Remove z only from targets that see every possible z-corner.
Do not choose an arbitrary pair of corners as endpoints. When three corners can hold z, the target must see all three.

Use this only for a uniquely solvable classic Sudoku. Every unsolved cell has two candidates except one cell with three. Removing one candidate from that cell would leave each unsolved digit occurring exactly twice in every house where it is still needed.

That fully bivalue pattern is a Binary Universal Grave: it cannot preserve a unique solution. The candidate whose removal would create it must instead be true, so place that digit in the three-candidate cell.
Check the whole board, not only the three-candidate cell. Having one trivalue cell is insufficient: the remaining house counts must form the complete BUG pattern.
The board now shows the proved changes. Placed digits also clear matching candidates from their peers; no further solving is applied. Return to the previous step to compare.
